say: This video explains how FacultyLens works, and what we used to build it.

FacultyLens has three parts. A React website that people use. A Python A P I, built with Fast A P I. And a Mongo D B database that stores users, forms, responses and results. The language models run inside the A P I, on an ordinary C P U, with no graphics card.

The website is built with React and Veet, using React Router for pages, Tailwind for the design system, and Re charts for the charts. Every number on screen comes from the A P I. The design follows our Affinity Wall idea: student comments become notes, pinned under the aspect they talk about. It meets W C A G double A contrast, and works with a keyboard, and in dark mode.

The A P I is written in Python, with Fast A P I and Pydantic. People sign in with short lived tokens, passwords are hashed with bcrypt, and repeated failed sign ins are slowed down. There are four roles: students, faculty, heads of department, and the admin admin. Every request checks the role before it answers.

Here is the journey of one comment. A student fills a form, with ratings from one to five, and a few lines in their own words. The response is saved without their name. A one way code, made with a secret key, only stops them from submitting the same form twice.

The analysis pipeline starts in the background. First, the text is cleaned, and personal details are removed. Our own rules catch Indian phone numbers, emails, and M V S R roll numbers, and the spacy language model catches names. Then the comment is split into sentences.

Next, pre-trained transformer models read every sentence. A toxicity model holds abusive comments back, for a person to review. A Roberta model scores sentiment, as positive, neutral, or negative. Two more models measure emotion and sarcasm, and possibly sarcastic praise counts only half.

Then comes our own method for teaching aspects. A sentence embedding model turns each sentence into numbers, and we compare them with example phrases we wrote for eight aspects, like clarity, punctuality, and pace. A Deberta model then decides whether that sentence praises, or criticises, the aspect.
Each model loads only the first time it is needed, runs in small batches on the C P U, and every result is saved, so no comment is ever analysed twice.

The results are added up for each teacher. The counts decide the strengths, and the areas to improve. A large language model from Grock only words the summary, and it must cite the exact comments behind every point. If it is not available, a local model writes it instead.
Privacy is built in. Teachers see only moderated, redacted text, and only after at least five students have answered. The bias check looks at whole departments, never at one teacher.

Finally, we measure how well it works. We trained classical models, like T F I D F with logistic regression, and compared them with the transformer. Annotators label comments to measure agreement, and summaries are scored with rouge, and Bert score. Over five hundred automated tests check the whole system.
That is FacultyLens. Every comment, sorted and heard. Built by Rohnith, Varshith and Akhil, at M V S R Engineering College.
